raw: 47.1 Evaluation Framework for ICS Cyber Incidents (ScienceDirect 2021)[^217]
teaching_note: A comparative incident framework organizes reported evidence; it cannot turn selected public cases into a representative frequency estimate. The cited paper's full methodology was unavailable in this review, so its exact scoring formula and validation remain unverified [@ageint217]. For a completed synthetic timeline, card A says '09:00 malware reported on an office computer' and card B says '09:05 service interruption'; arranging them chronologically establishes sequence, not causation. Card C then identifies a planned outage starting at 08:55, so the reviewer withdraws the draft cyber-caused-outage conclusion, records the alternative, and stops attribution pending independent causal evidence, using Section [@sec:analytic-workflow].
title: Evaluation Framework for ICS Cyber Incidents (ScienceDirect 2021)

raw: 47.2 The Cyber-Physical Six: Stuxnet, BlackEnergy, CrashOverride, Trisis, Irongate, Havex[^218]
teaching_note: The inherited heading combines two different case selections and must not be read as Honeywell's table of contents. Honeywell's report selects Stuxnet, BlackEnergy, Industroyer, Trisis, Industroyer 2, and Incontroller; the curriculum's retained Irongate and Havex topics belong to a different comparison [@ageint218; @ageint217]. Its time-bound claims about known capabilities are not a current exhaustive census. Compare each case by reported observation, inferred capability, demonstrated physical effect, simulation status, attribution source, and unresolved claims; do not flatten these into six equivalent destructive incidents.
title: Comparing Selected Cases with Honeywell's Different Cyber-Physical Six

raw: 47.2.1 Stuxnet: First Cyber-Physical Weapon — Operation Olympic Games[^219][^220]
teaching_note: Stuxnet is a landmark reported industrial sabotage case, but 'first' depends on the definition and historical evidence, and an operation name is an attribution claim rather than an observation from code alone [@ageint219; @ageint220]. Separate technical behavior, reported equipment consequences, and accounts of sponsorship. Historical reporting supports a bounded case discussion, not a claim that every infection caused physical damage or that a similar alert identifies the same sponsor.
title: Stuxnet: Reported Physical Sabotage and Attributed Operation Context

teaching_note: Honeywell describes the 2015 campaign as coordinated activity involving remote access, credential misuse, destructive components, and interference with response; the malware family name is shorthand for the campaign, not a complete causal account [@ageint218]. Distinguish malware presence from the actions reported to produce the outage. The defensive lesson is to examine human, communications, and process dependencies together, without reproducing the campaign or extrapolating a universal loss estimate.
title: BlackEnergy: Ukraine Power Grid Attacks (2015)

teaching_note: The inherited 'protocol-agnostic' description is misleading: Honeywell describes modules designed for particular industrial protocols [@ageint218]. Modularity or portability does not eliminate dependence on protocol semantics, installation configuration, and process context. Interpret a claimed capability separately from a demonstrated deployment and observed physical consequence; no protocol interaction or executable demonstration is needed.
title: CrashOverride/Industroyer: Protocol-aware Modular Industrial Malware

teaching_note: A safety instrumented system serves a protective function distinct from ordinary process control; targeting that protection changes the potential hazard even when a public report does not establish a destructive outcome [@ageint218]. Distinguish attempted impairment, confirmed modification, loss of protection, and actual harm. Neither a reported safety-system target nor a synthetic representation permits students to test, alter, or bypass any protective system.
title: Triton/Trisis: Safety Instrumented System Attack

raw: 47.2.5 Irongate: Stuxnet Descendant Against Simulated Environment[^217]
teaching_note: Resemblance to Stuxnet-like concepts does not establish code ancestry, shared authorship, or operational deployment. The inherited 'descendant' wording is therefore not adopted; the cited comparative source is retained as provenance, while operational applicability and genealogy remain unsupported here [@ageint217]. A simulation or proof-of-concept observation cannot establish a real plant compromise or measured physical effect, and this lesson does not recreate one.
title: Irongate: Reported Simulated-environment Case, Lineage Unestablished

raw: 47.2.6 Havex: IT-OT Pivot Using Weaponized OPC Software[^217]
teaching_note: Industrial reconnaissance, access to process-related information, and physical manipulation are different claims. Honeywell explicitly excludes the Dragonfly reconnaissance campaign from its own six-case physical-impact selection, so its discussion cannot support treating every Havex-related report as a demonstrated destructive event [@ageint218]. The inherited OPC-software description requires source-specific verification before making delivery or causal assertions; retain it as historical source identity rather than a deployment recipe.
title: Havex: Reported Industrial Reconnaissance and Evidence Boundaries

raw: 47.3 Threat Scoring Framework: Malware Sophistication × Attack Consequence[^217]
teaching_note: Sophistication and consequence are separate dimensions: a simple action in a dependent process can have serious consequences, while elaborate code may have no demonstrated physical effect. In an explicitly fictional comparison, case A has 'simple mechanism / service interruption reported' and case B has 'complex mechanism / consequence unknown'; the correct output is two descriptive rows, not a numerical risk ranking. Multiplying ordinal labels has no justified quantitative meaning, and the unavailable full methodology of the cited framework prevents reproducing an exact source formula [@ageint217]. The reviewer holds prioritization until consequence evidence and applicable scales are supplied; these classroom judgments are not calibrated risk or expected-loss estimates.
title: Comparing Malware Sophistication and Reported Consequence without an Unverified Formula
